problem: Hindsight Experience Replay (HER) needs a state-to-goal mapping and UVFA goal substitution, so it cannot be applied to visual tasks where goal states look visually distinct and the policy sees only the state image. Sparse-reward visual RL therefore wastes millions of steps on failed trajectories.
motivation: Sample complexity is a major barrier to training RL in the real world, where data collection is costly. Failed visual trajectories could be reused if the goal could be visually inserted into the observations consistently along the trajectory.
key_idea: Train a conditional Wasserstein ACGAN (HALGAN) on a few goal snapshots with known relative pose to add minimal, pose-consistent goal hallucinations to failed trajectories, then combine it with HER so the agent gets hindsight reward.
insight: Hallucinating goals into failed trajectories gives the agent reward signal from the start, whereas naive HER, VAE-based dense rewards (vae-her, rig-) and plain DDPG/DDQN mostly fail or learn slowly. The additive generator plus L2 penalty keeps hallucinations minimal, and the model needs little data: shrinking R to 1000 images on TurtleBot only slows learning slightly (Fig. 5f). Results are shown only as learning curves, not tables.
method: Additive minimal hallucination: the generator H outputs only a difference image added to the failed state, s̄_t = tanh(s_t + H(c(s_t; s_T), l)), so background and dynamics are preserved.
Relative-pose conditioning: H is conditioned on the agent's pose relative to a future state's pose (x, y, yaw), giving temporal consistency across the trajectory without modeling sequences.

W-ACGAN with regression auxiliary task: WGAN-GP loss, plus an L2 penalty on H's output (to remove extra goals or walls), plus an MSE loss so D regresses the goal's relative pose (weights 10/1/10 for GP/L2/aux).
Goal-snapshot data: R is the last 16 or 32 states of successful rollouts, auto-annotated with relative pose from the agent configuration (1k–7k images). Failed states come from the replay warmup.

HALGAN+HER training (Alg. 1): with probability p (annealed from 20–30% to 0), sample a future state at offset d, hallucinate the goal into s_i and s_{i+1}, and reassign a sparse +1 reward if the agent pose matches the pose at s_{i+d} within a threshold. Off-policy learners are DDQN (discrete) and DDPG (continuous).
Baselines: her (relabel final states without hallucination), vae-her and rig- (VAE dense rewards derived from RIG).

setting.backbone: Small CNN policies (DDQN / DDPG actor-critic, ~33K params each) trained from scratch, plus a W-ACGAN (HALGAN) trained from scratch
setting.model_size: ~33K-parameter policy; HALGAN generator ~324K and discriminator ~330K parameters
setting.training_data: Sparse-reward RL from scratch; HALGAN trained on 6,840 (TurtleBot), 2,000 (MiniWorld navigate) and 6,419 (MiniWorld successive navigation) goal snapshots with relative pose
setting.observation: monocular RGB 64x64 image; agent pose (x, y, yaw) used only for hallucination and reward reassignment
setting.action_space: Discrete (4 actions, TurtleBot) and continuous 2-D control (MiniWorld)
setting.privileged: Agent configuration/pose during training (as if from SLAM), plus pose-annotated goal snapshots used to train HALGAN

numbers_note: Results are given only as learning curves in figures (episodic reward vs. steps); no numeric tables. The tasks are custom, not standard navigation benchmarks.
results: HALGAN+HER agents begin learning immediately in all three tasks. In the MiniWorld tasks only HALGAN learns reliably, while rig- succeeds on some seeds of navigation and one seed of successive navigation. On TurtleBot, HALGAN beats the DDQN, her and rig- baselines, and reducing HALGAN's data to 1000 images costs little.
limitations: Needs pose-annotated goal snapshots and a reliable agent pose estimate; the hallucinator is conditioned only on relative pose, so it ignores lighting, occlusion and background cues.
Evaluated only in simple, small simulated environments with a single goal object and 3-5 seeds; no real robot; results are only curves.
